why: Most Power BI interviews for analyst roles go past SUM and a year-to-date: they ask why a total looks wrong, how CALCULATE treats a slicer, how to rank or compare periods correctly and how to make a slow report fast. Mastering evaluation contexts is what separates someone who copies measures from someone who can write and debug them.
outcome: reason about row and filter context, control CALCULATE and context transition, write correct time intelligence, ranking, Top N, new-customer, Pareto and closing-balance measures, use relationships from DAX, and diagnose and organise a model with DAX Studio, calculation groups and clear naming.

lessons.title: Evaluation contexts for real: row context, filter context and what a visual sends
text: Every DAX expression runs in two possible contexts. The filter context is the set of filters active on model columns: it decides which rows of Sales a measure sees. The row context exists only while DAX iterates a table, row by row: in a calculated column or inside an iterator such as SUMX. The key fact interviews test is that a row context does not filter anything. A calculated column Sales All Customers = SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] ) on the Customer table returns the grand total on every row, because iterating Customer does not filter Sales.

A visual builds the filter context for you. For a matrix with Product[Category] on rows and 'Date'[Year] on columns, Power BI sends one DAX query (built with SUMMARIZECOLUMNS) and every cell is evaluated with the filters of its row and column, plus slicers, page and report filters and visual-level filters. Filters on Product then flow through the one-to-many relationship to Sales. Rows where every measure returns blank are removed from the result, which is why empty categories disappear.

The total row is not a sum of the rows above it. It is the same measure evaluated again with fewer filters: the category filter is simply absent. For an additive measure like Sales Amount both match; for Customers (a distinct count) or an average they do not, since a customer who bought bikes and helmets counts once in the total. This is correct behaviour, not a bug, and you must explain it to users.

To debug a measure, look at its context. Put it in a matrix next to the dimension, compute one cell by hand, then inspect the context with ISINSCOPE (is this column grouping the current cell, which tells detail rows from totals), HASONEVALUE and SELECTEDVALUE. DAX query view in Power BI Desktop and DAX Studio let you run EVALUATE queries and see exactly what a measure returns.
points: Filter context = which rows a measure sees; row context = the current row of an iteration.
A row context does not filter related tables: only CALCULATE (context transition) turns it into a filter.
Each cell of a visual is a separate evaluation with its own filter context.
Totals are re-evaluated, not summed: distinct counts and averages are not additive.
ISINSCOPE tells a detail row from a total; SELECTEDVALUE returns the single value or blank.

example.code:
-- Calculated columns on Customer (row context, computed at refresh)
Sales All Customers = SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] )            -- grand total on every row
Customer Sales = CALCULATE ( SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] ) )   -- this customer's sales

-- Measures (filter context, computed for every cell of a visual)
Sales Amount = SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] )

Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Sales[CustomerKey] )

Sales per Customer = DIVIDE ( [Sales Amount], [Customers] )

Category Label =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( Product[Category] ),
    SELECTEDVALUE ( Product[Category] ),
    "All categories"
)
example.note: Customers on the total row is lower than the sum of the category rows: customers who bought in several categories are counted once. Sales per Customer at total level is therefore not the average of the rows either.

lessons.title: CALCULATE in depth: filter arguments, KEEPFILTERS and context transition
text: CALCULATE follows a precise order. It evaluates its filter arguments in the original filter context, then turns any row context into filters (context transition), then applies modifiers such as REMOVEFILTERS, USERELATIONSHIP or CROSSFILTER, then applies the filter arguments, and only then evaluates the expression. A boolean filter like Product[Color] = "Red" is shorthand for FILTER ( ALL ( Product[Color] ), Product[Color] = "Red" ): it replaces any existing filter on that column. In a matrix by colour, Red Sales shows red sales on the Blue row.

KEEPFILTERS changes replace into intersect: the Blue row then shows blank, and a slicer on Red and Blue keeps working. Neither is wrong; it depends on the question. "Red sales, whatever the colour selected" needs the plain filter, "sales of the selection that are red" needs KEEPFILTERS. Ask the business user which one they mean before writing it.

Removing filters has several tools. REMOVEFILTERS (a modifier, the clearest name) and ALL clear filters on a table or columns; ALL can also return a table. ALLEXCEPT ( Product, Product[Category] ) clears every Product filter except the category, but also removes a brand slicer. ALLSELECTED restores the filters coming from outside the visual (slicers, page filters) while removing those of the visual's rows and columns: use it for a percentage of the visible total.

Context transition happens whenever CALCULATE runs in a row context, and every measure reference carries an implicit CALCULATE. It is what makes MAXX ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Sales Amount] ) work per customer. Two costs come with it: it is expensive on large tables, and on a table without a unique key it filters every identical row, so SUMX ( Sales, [Sales Amount] ) can double count duplicate lines. Iterate a dimension or a column of keys, not the fact table.
points: Filter arguments are evaluated in the original context, before context transition.
A boolean filter overwrites filters on its column; KEEPFILTERS intersects with them.
REMOVEFILTERS for clarity, ALLEXCEPT keeps chosen columns, ALLSELECTED keeps the outer selection.
Every measure reference inside an iterator triggers context transition.
Never iterate the fact table with a measure: iterate keys of a dimension.

example.code:
Red Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], Product[Color] = "Red" )

Red Sales (keep filters) =
CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], KEEPFILTERS ( Product[Color] = "Red" ) )

% of All Categories =
DIVIDE (
    [Sales Amount],
    CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] ) )
)

% of Visible Total =
DIVIDE ( [Sales Amount], CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], ALLSELECTED () ) )

Category Sales (all products) =
CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], ALLEXCEPT ( Product, Product[Category] ) )
example.note: REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] ) clears only that column: put Product[Subcategory] on rows and the subcategory filter stays, so every row shows 100 %. Remove the columns that are actually on the visual.

lessons.title: Iterators and variables: computing at the right grain
text: An iterator (SUMX, AVERAGEX, MINX, MAXX, COUNTX, RANKX, FILTER) creates a row context over a table, evaluates an expression for each row, and aggregates the results. SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] ) is in fact shorthand for SUMX ( Sales, Sales[NetAmount] ). You need an explicit iterator when the calculation must happen before the aggregation, such as quantity times price, or at another grain than the visual.

Choosing the table to iterate chooses the grain. AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( 'Date'[YearMonth] ), [Sales Amount] ) is the average monthly sales of the period, whatever the visual shows; MAXX ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Sales Amount] ) is the best customer's sales. Iterate the smallest table that has the grain you need: a few thousand customers, not fifty million order lines.

FILTER is an iterator that returns a table, and it is the tool when a condition needs a measure, because a boolean filter argument in CALCULATE cannot reference a measure. COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Sales Amount] > 1000 ) ) counts customers above 1,000. But FILTER ( Sales, … ) on a whole fact table, or FILTER ( ALL ( Product ), … ) used as a CALCULATE argument, is slow and also removes filters you may want to keep: filter columns, not tables.

VAR … RETURN makes measures readable and faster, because each variable is evaluated once. A variable is evaluated where it is defined, in the context of that moment, and then it is a constant: CALCULATE ( CurrentSales, 'Date'[Year] = 2025 ) returns the current sales, not 2025. Use variables for values you reuse, and to debug: RETURN one intermediate variable to see what it holds.
points: SUM(column) = SUMX(table, column): iterators are the general form.
The iterated table sets the grain: months, customers, stores.
Use FILTER over a dimension when the condition needs a measure.
A VAR is evaluated once, where it is defined, and never changes afterwards.
RETURN an intermediate variable to debug a long measure.

example.code:
Avg Monthly Sales =
AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( 'Date'[YearMonth] ), [Sales Amount] )

Best Customer Sales =
MAXX ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Sales Amount] )

Customers over 1000 =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Sales Amount] > 1000 )
)

Sales vs PY Label =
VAR CurrentSales = [Sales Amount]
VAR PreviousSales =
    CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], DATEADD ( 'Date'[Date], -1, YEAR ) )
RETURN
    SWITCH (
        TRUE (),
        ISBLANK ( CurrentSales ), BLANK (),
        ISBLANK ( PreviousSales ), "New",
        FORMAT ( DIVIDE ( CurrentSales - PreviousSales, PreviousSales ), "0.0%" )
    )

-- Wrong: a variable is a constant, CALCULATE cannot change it
Sales 2025 (wrong) =
VAR CurrentSales = [Sales Amount]
RETURN CALCULATE ( CurrentSales, 'Date'[Year] = 2025 )
example.note: Sales 2025 (wrong) returns the current sales because CurrentSales was computed before CALCULATE. Write CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], 'Date'[Year] = 2025 ) instead. The ISBLANK test on CurrentSales keeps rows without sales out of the visual.

lessons.title: Time intelligence done right: date table, YTD, prior year and rolling periods
text: Time intelligence functions return a set of dates that CALCULATE uses as a filter, so they depend on the date table. It needs one row per day with no gaps, whole years, a unique Date column, and Mark as date table. When a time intelligence filter is applied on 'Date'[Date], DAX removes the other filters on 'Date' (year, month) so the shifted dates are not intersected with the current ones; marking the table guarantees this even when the relationship uses an integer key. Always pass 'Date'[Date], never Sales[OrderDate].

TOTALYTD and DATESYTD accept a year-end date for fiscal years: TOTALYTD ( [Sales Amount], 'Date'[Date], "06-30" ) for a year ending on 30 June. Add FiscalYear and FiscalMonth columns to the date table for the axis. Retail calendars of 4-4-5 weeks do not fit the classic functions: use week columns and your own filters, or the calendar-based time intelligence introduced in preview in late 2025 (check its status in your Desktop version).

Prior-year comparisons hide a trap. If data stops on 31 October 2026 while the date table runs to December, the 2026 total compares ten months with twelve months of 2025, and YoY looks terrible. Add a DateWithSales column to the date table and restrict the dates before shifting them. In YoY %, return blank when either year is blank, so new products do not show +∞ or -100 %.

Rolling periods use DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -12, MONTH ): the last visible date, going back 12 months. MAX is evaluated in the original context because filter arguments are computed before CALCULATE applies them. DATEADD shifts the visible dates by a number of days, months, quarters or years and works at any level of the visual.
points: Date table: every day, whole years, unique dates, marked as date table, auto date/time off.
Always use 'Date'[Date] in time intelligence functions, not a fact column.
Fiscal year: pass the year-end date, e.g. "06-30", to TOTALYTD or DATESYTD.
Limit prior-year comparisons to dates that already have data.
Rolling 12 months = DATESINPERIOD ending at the last visible date.

example.code:
-- Calculated column in 'Date': DateWithSales = 'Date'[Date] <= MAX ( Sales[OrderDate] )

Sales YTD = TOTALYTD ( [Sales Amount], 'Date'[Date] )

Sales FYTD = TOTALYTD ( [Sales Amount], 'Date'[Date], "06-30" )

Sales PY =
CALCULATE (
    [Sales Amount],
    CALCULATETABLE (
        SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ),
        'Date'[DateWithSales] = TRUE
    )
)

Sales YoY % =
VAR Cur = [Sales Amount]
VAR Prev = [Sales PY]
RETURN IF ( ISBLANK ( Cur ) || ISBLANK ( Prev ), BLANK (), DIVIDE ( Cur - Prev, Prev ) )

Sales R12M =
CALCULATE (
    [Sales Amount],
    DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -12, MONTH )
)
example.note: The CALCULATETABLE keeps only the current dates that have sales before shifting them one year back, so 2026 (to October) is compared with January to October 2025, not the whole of 2025.

lessons.title: Ranking and Top N: RANKX, ties and the "Others" row
text: RANKX ( table, expression, value, order, ties ) evaluates the expression for each row of the table (a measure triggers context transition), then evaluates it once more in the current context and returns its position. The table must contain all the competitors: with VALUES ( Product[Product Name] ) the table only holds the current product, so every product ranks 1. ALL ( Product[Product Name] ) ranks against every product name, even those left out by a slicer or filter on that column; ALLSELECTED ranks within the names the user selected. Filters on other tables, such as the year or the store, still apply.

Ties use SKIP by default (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE gives 1, 2, 2, 3. Rank on a unique column: two products sharing a name would be merged into one. Return blank on the total row with ISINSCOPE, and decide whether products without sales should be ranked at all. The window functions RANK, ROWNUMBER, INDEX and OFFSET (added in 2022–2023) rank with explicit ORDERBY and PARTITIONBY and are worth knowing, but RANKX remains the most common in existing models.

"Top 5 products and Others" is a classic request. The visual needs a row called Others that does not exist in Product, so you create a calculated table of the names plus "Others", not related to the model, and put its column on rows. The measure returns the sales of a name when it is in the top 5, the sales of all the other products on the Others row, and blank elsewhere so the visual hides the rest.

TOPN ( 5, table, expression, DESC ) returns the top rows as a table you can reuse as a filter or with EXCEPT. It returns more than 5 rows when there is a tie at the fifth position, so say how ties are handled when you show the result.
points: RANKX needs the full list of competitors: ALL or ALLSELECTED, never VALUES alone.
ALL ignores a selection on the ranked column; ALLSELECTED ranks within it.
Ties: SKIP (default) or DENSE.
Blank the rank on totals with ISINSCOPE.
TOPN can return more than N rows when values tie.

example.code:
Product Rank =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product Name] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( Product[Product Name] ), [Sales Amount], , DESC, DENSE )
)

-- Calculated table, not related to anything: every name plus an "Others" row
Product Ranking = UNION ( DISTINCT ( Product[Product Name] ), { "Others" } )

Top 5 + Others =
VAR AllNames = ALLSELECTED ( Product[Product Name] )
VAR TopProducts = TOPN ( 5, AllNames, [Sales Amount], DESC )
VAR CurrentName = SELECTEDVALUE ( 'Product Ranking'[Product Name] )
RETURN
    SWITCH (
        TRUE (),
        NOT ISINSCOPE ( 'Product Ranking'[Product Name] ), [Sales Amount],
        CurrentName = "Others",
            CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], EXCEPT ( AllNames, TopProducts ) ),
        CurrentName IN TopProducts,
            CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], TREATAS ( { CurrentName }, Product[Product Name] ) )
    )
example.note: The visual sorts by sales, so Others may appear at the top when the tail is large. Add a sort measure (rank, with Others last) or sort by a column. A real product named "Others" would break the pattern.

lessons.title: Relationships in DAX: USERELATIONSHIP, CROSSFILTER and TREATAS
text: Sales has two dates, OrderDate and DeliveryDate, but only one relationship between 'Date' and Sales can be active. Keep OrderDate active, create the DeliveryDate relationship as inactive, and use USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE in the measures that need it: the active relationship is ignored while that measure runs. If users must filter by order date and delivery date at the same time (ordered in January, delivered in February), a second date dimension is simpler than measures.

Relationships filter from the one side to the many side. Setting a relationship to both directions in the model is tempting but creates ambiguous paths and slows every query. CROSSFILTER ( Sales[ProductKey], Product[ProductKey], BOTH ) enables both directions for a single measure, for example to count the brands bought by the selected customers; NONE switches a relationship off inside one calculation.

TREATAS applies the values of a table as filters on columns of another table: a virtual relationship. A typical case is a budget stored per Category and YearMonth with no relationship to the model, because its grain is coarser than Product and 'Date'. TREATAS ( VALUES ( Product[Category] ), Budget[Category] ) moves the category selection onto the budget. It is cleaner and faster than FILTER or INTERSECT patterns, but a physical relationship to a shared Category dimension remains faster and is easier for report authors.

Many-to-many relationships, where neither side has unique values, are allowed in Power BI but easy to misread. Below the budget grain, every product of a category shows the full category budget, and totals are not the sum of the rows. Show such measures only at their grain, for example with ISINSCOPE, and document it. Bridge tables with bidirectional filters, such as customers sharing accounts, give non-additive totals: test them on a small sample.
points: One active relationship between two tables; activate others with USERELATIONSHIP.
CROSSFILTER changes direction (BOTH, ONEWAY, NONE) for one measure only.
TREATAS creates a virtual relationship: values must match in type and format.
Prefer a shared dimension to TREATAS when the model is used by many reports.
Show many-to-many results only at the grain where they make sense.

example.code:
-- Model: 'Date'[Date] -> Sales[OrderDate] (active), 'Date'[Date] -> Sales[DeliveryDate] (inactive)
Sales by Delivery Date =
CALCULATE (
    [Sales Amount],
    USERELATIONSHIP ( Sales[DeliveryDate], 'Date'[Date] )
)

Brands Bought =
CALCULATE (
    DISTINCTCOUNT ( Product[Brand] ),
    CROSSFILTER ( Sales[ProductKey], Product[ProductKey], BOTH )
)

-- Budget (Category, YearMonth, Amount) has no relationship in the model
Budget Amount =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( Budget[Amount] ),
    TREATAS ( VALUES ( Product[Category] ), Budget[Category] ),
    TREATAS ( VALUES ( 'Date'[YearMonth] ), Budget[YearMonth] )
)
example.note: TREATAS compares values exactly: store YearMonth as the same integer (202611) in 'Date' and Budget. Without CROSSFILTER, Brands Bought would count every brand, because Sales does not filter Product.

lessons.title: Virtual tables and advanced patterns: new customers, Pareto and closing balances
text: A measure can build tables in memory and then aggregate them. VALUES returns the visible values of a column, ADDCOLUMNS adds computed columns to a table (a measure inside it triggers context transition), and FILTER keeps the rows you need. SUMMARIZECOLUMNS is what visuals use in their queries and the best choice in DAX queries and calculated tables; inside measures, ADDCOLUMNS over VALUES is the safe, classic pattern. Name virtual columns with a prefix such as @FirstDate so they are not confused with model columns.

New customers: a customer is new in a period when their first purchase ever falls in it. Take the customers who bought in the period, add their first order date computed with REMOVEFILTERS ( 'Date' ), and count those whose first date is on or after the period start. Returning customers are the rest. Other filters stay: with a Bikes slicer, "new" means new to bikes, so agree on the definition with the business.

ABC or Pareto analysis ranks products by sales and accumulates their share: class A makes the first 80 % of sales, B the next 15 %, C the rest. As a measure it reacts to slicers (top products of this store this year); as a calculated column it is fixed at refresh but fast and usable as a slicer. Products with equal sales get the same cumulative share.

Balances, stock levels and headcount are semi-additive: they add up across stores and products but not across time. Summing a daily stock snapshot over a month gives a meaningless number; the closing stock is the value on the last date. LASTDATE returns the last date of the period even if no snapshot exists that day, LASTNONBLANK returns the last date with data. Here a Stock snapshot table (Date, StoreKey, ProductKey, UnitsOnHand) joins the model.
points: Virtual tables: VALUES, ADDCOLUMNS, FILTER, then COUNTROWS or SUMX.
New customer = first purchase ever (REMOVEFILTERS on dates) inside the period.
Pareto: cumulative share of sales over products sorted by sales.
Semi-additive: sum across stores, take the last value across time.
LASTDATE = last date of the period; LASTNONBLANK = last date with data.

example.code:
New Customers =
VAR PeriodStart = MIN ( 'Date'[Date] )
VAR FirstPurchases =
    ADDCOLUMNS (
        VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ),
        "@FirstDate", CALCULATE ( MIN ( Sales[OrderDate] ), REMOVEFILTERS ( 'Date' ) )
    )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( FirstPurchases, [@FirstDate] >= PeriodStart ) )

Returning Customers = [Customers] - [New Customers]

-- Stock: one row per Date, StoreKey, ProductKey with UnitsOnHand (daily snapshot)
Closing Stock =
VAR LastStockDate =
    LASTNONBLANK ( 'Date'[Date], CALCULATE ( SUM ( Stock[UnitsOnHand] ) ) )
RETURN
    CALCULATE ( SUM ( Stock[UnitsOnHand] ), LastStockDate )
example.note: At the all-stores level LASTNONBLANK finds one date for everyone: a store whose last snapshot is a day earlier drops out of the total. Compute the closing stock per store and add them up (see the exercises).

lessons.title: Performance and maintainability: engines, DAX Studio and calculation groups
text: A query runs on two engines. The storage engine (VertiPaq in Import mode) scans compressed columns, is multi-threaded and caches results; the formula engine is single-threaded and handles everything the storage engine cannot, such as complex IF logic or context transition row by row. Fast DAX pushes work to the storage engine. Model size still matters: high-cardinality columns are what you remove first.

Measure, don't guess. Performance Analyzer shows which visual is slow; copy its query into DAX Studio, clear the cache and run it with Server Timings. A large formula engine share, or hundreds of storage engine queries, points to an iteration with context transition over a big table; CallbackDataID in a storage engine query means it had to call the formula engine for each row. Change one thing at a time and compare.

Habits that pay: filter columns, not whole tables (KEEPFILTERS ( Sales[Quantity] >= 10 ) instead of FILTER ( Sales, … )); iterate dimension keys, not the fact table; store reused results in variables; use DIVIDE for divisions that can hit zero; do not turn blanks into zeros everywhere, since a measure that never returns blank forces visuals to show every combination of rows.

Maintainability is part of the job. Calculation groups, now authorable in Power BI Desktop's model view, apply YTD, PY or YoY % to any measure through SELECTEDMEASURE, instead of three copies of every measure; they affect every measure in the visual, so exclude ratios with ISSELECTEDMEASURE when needed, and plan explicit measures, as creating one can turn on the Discourage implicit measures setting. Field parameters let users switch measures or columns in a visual (long a preview feature: check your version). Keep base measures in a dedicated measures table with display folders, consistent names (Sales Amount, Sales PY, Sales YoY %), format strings and descriptions.
points: Storage engine: fast, parallel, cached; formula engine: single-threaded.
Performance Analyzer finds the visual; DAX Studio Server Timings explains it.
Filter columns, not tables; never iterate the fact table with a measure.
Calculation groups replace families of time measures with SELECTEDMEASURE.
A measures table, display folders and consistent names make a model usable by others.

example.code:
-- Slow: FILTER iterates the whole Sales table
Big Order Sales (slow) =
CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], FILTER ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] >= 10 ) )

-- Fast: a filter on one column, same result
Big Order Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], KEEPFILTERS ( Sales[Quantity] >= 10 ) )

-- Calculation group "Time Calc": one DAX expression per calculation item
-- Item "Current"
SELECTEDMEASURE ()
-- Item "YTD"
CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), DATESYTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
-- Item "PY"
CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
-- Item "YoY %" (format string expression: "0.0%")
VAR Cur = SELECTEDMEASURE ()
VAR Prev = CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
RETURN DIVIDE ( Cur - Prev, Prev )
example.note: The YoY % item would also apply to a measure that is already a percentage and give a meaningless result: test with ISSELECTEDMEASURE or SELECTEDMEASURENAME and return SELECTEDMEASURE () unchanged for such measures.

items: Filters active on model columns: which rows a measure sees
The current row of an iteration; it does not filter other tables
TRUE when the cell is grouped by this column (not a total)
The single visible value, or the alternate value
TRUE when exactly one value of the column is visible
Replaces any existing filter on Color
Intersects the new filter with the existing one
Clears the filters on one column inside CALCULATE
Clears every Product filter except the category
Keeps outer filters (slicers), drops the visual's own
CALCULATE turns the current row into filters
Evaluate once, where defined; a constant afterwards
Fiscal year to date, year ending 30 June
Visible dates shifted one year back
Visible dates shifted one quarter back
Last 12 months up to the last visible date
Lets time intelligence remove other date filters, even with an integer key
Rank against every product name, even unselected ones
Ties share a rank with no gap: 1, 2, 2, 3
Top 5 rows as a table, more if tied
Rows of table1 that are not in table2 (the Others)
Use an inactive relationship in one measure
Filter in both directions for one measure
Virtual relationship to an unrelated table
Neither side unique: show results only at its grain
Add a computed column to a virtual table
Last date that has stock data
Last date of the period, data or not
Adds up across stores, not across time
Storage engine vs formula engine time and queries
The storage engine calls the formula engine row by row
The measure a calculation item is applied to
Exclude some measures from a calculation item
One place to find every measure

pitfalls: Ranking with RANKX over VALUES of the current column, so every row ranks 1: rank over ALL or ALLSELECTED of the column.
Using a boolean filter in CALCULATE when the user expects the slicer to apply: wrap it in KEEPFILTERS.
Writing FILTER ( Sales, … ) as a CALCULATE argument on a fact table of millions of rows: filter the column instead.
Iterating the fact table with a measure (SUMX ( Sales, [Margin] )): context transition per row is slow and double counts duplicate lines; use columns or iterate a dimension.
Comparing a partial current year with a full prior year: restrict the dates to those with data before shifting them.
Passing Sales[OrderDate] to time intelligence functions or using an unmarked date table with gaps: use a complete, marked 'Date' table.
Summing a stock or balance over months: use a closing balance with LASTNONBLANK, computed per store.
Adding + 0 or IF ( ISBLANK (…), 0 ) to every measure: visuals then show every combination and become slow.

exercises.q: A matrix shows Product[Category] then Product[Product Name] on rows. Write a measure for the share of each product in the sales of its category.
exercises.hint: Keep the category filter, remove only the product filter in the denominator.
exercises.answer:
Share in Category =
DIVIDE (
    [Sales Amount],
    CALCULATE ( [Sales Amount], REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Product Name] ) )
)
exercises.explain: On a product row, the denominator removes the product name filter but keeps the category of the row, so it returns the category total. Use ALLSELECTED ( Product[Product Name] ) instead if a slicer on product names should limit the denominator too.

exercises.q: Write a measure for the average monthly sales of the last 3 months, ending at the last visible date (so it works by month in a line chart).
exercises.hint: DATESINPERIOD gives the dates; AVERAGEX over months gives the monthly average.
exercises.answer:
Sales 3M Avg =
VAR LastVisibleDate = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
VAR Last3Months = DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], LastVisibleDate, -3, MONTH )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( 'Date'[YearMonth] ), [Sales Amount] ),
        Last3Months
    )
exercises.explain: The filter on 'Date'[Date] replaces the visual's month filter (the date table is marked), so VALUES ( 'Date'[YearMonth] ) returns the three months and AVERAGEX averages their sales.

exercises.q: In a matrix with Product[Category] and Product[Product Name] on rows, write a rank of each product within its category, using only the products the user selected, with dense ties and blank on total rows.
exercises.answer:
Rank in Category =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product Name] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( Product[Product Name] ), [Sales Amount], , DESC, DENSE )
)
exercises.explain: ALLSELECTED removes the product name filter of the row but keeps the category of the outer row and the slicers, so the rank is computed within the category. ISINSCOPE hides it on category and grand totals.

exercises.q: [Closing Stock] uses LASTNONBLANK on 'Date'[Date]. At the all-stores level the total is too low because some stores sent their last snapshot a day earlier. Write a measure that gives the correct total.
exercises.hint: Compute the closing stock store by store, then add up.
exercises.answer:
Closing Stock (all stores) =
SUMX ( VALUES ( Store[StoreKey] ), [Closing Stock] )
exercises.explain: SUMX iterates the stores and [Closing Stock] runs for each one (context transition), so each store uses its own last snapshot date before the results are summed.

exercises.q: This measure is slow on 40 million rows: Margin = SUMX ( Sales, [Line Margin] ), where [Line Margin] is a measure computing NetAmount minus Quantity times the product's UnitCost. Rewrite it.
exercises.hint: Avoid calling a measure for every row of the fact table.
exercises.answer:
Margin =
SUMX (
    Sales,
    Sales[NetAmount] - Sales[Quantity] * RELATED ( Product[UnitCost] )
)
exercises.explain: Referencing a measure inside SUMX over Sales triggers a context transition for every row: slow, and wrong when two lines are identical. Columns and RELATED keep the work in the storage engine.

exercises.q: A matrix has Product[Color] on rows and no slicer. What does the Red Sales measure show on the Blue row?
exercises.answer: The boolean filter replaces the existing filter on Product[Color] (Blue) with Red, so every row shows red sales. Wrap it in KEEPFILTERS to intersect instead: the Blue row is then blank.

exercises.q: Complete the rolling 12 months measure.
exercises.answer: MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ) is the last visible date, evaluated before CALCULATE applies the new filter; DATESINPERIOD then returns the 12 months ending on it.

exercises.q: Every product gets rank 1. Tap the line with the bug.
exercises.snippet:
Product Rank =
RANKX (
    VALUES ( Product[Product Name] ),
    [Sales Amount],
    ,
    DESC
)
exercises.fix:
Product Rank =
RANKX (
    ALLSELECTED ( Product[Product Name] ),
    [Sales Amount],
    ,
    DESC
)
exercises.answer: VALUES ( Product[Product Name] ) in a product row contains only the current product, so it is always first. RANKX needs the list of all competitors: ALLSELECTED (within the selection) or ALL (every product).

exercises.q: Match each need with the DAX function that solves it.
pairs: Analyse sales by delivery date with an inactive relationship
Let Sales filter Product in a single measure
Filter a budget table that has no relationship
Respect the slicer on a column you also filter
Percentage of the total the user selected
Closing stock on the last date with data
exercises.answer: USERELATIONSHIP and CROSSFILTER change relationships inside CALCULATE, TREATAS creates a virtual one, KEEPFILTERS and ALLSELECTED control how filters combine, and LASTNONBLANK handles semi-additive measures.

exercises.q: A sales manager complains that a matrix of customers by month takes 12 seconds to load.

choices.label: Performance Analyzer, then copy the slow visual's query into DAX Studio
choices.feedback: Right: find the slow visual, then measure its query with a cold cache and Server Timings.

choices.label: Rewrite every measure of the report
choices.feedback: Too broad: without measuring you may rewrite measures that are not the problem.

choices.label: Set every relationship to both directions
choices.feedback: This usually makes queries slower and results ambiguous.

steps.text: Server Timings: 85 % formula engine, 3,000 storage engine queries with CallbackDataID. The measure is SUMX ( Sales, [Line Margin] ). What do you change?

choices.label: Compute the margin from columns: SUMX ( Sales, Sales[NetAmount] - Sales[Quantity] * RELATED ( Product[UnitCost] ) )
choices.feedback: Right: no context transition per row, the storage engine can do the work.

choices.label: Add a page-level filter on the current year
choices.feedback: It hides the problem for this page only; the measure stays slow.

choices.label: Wrap the measure in IFERROR
choices.feedback: IFERROR does not make anything faster and can slow evaluation down.

steps.text: The visual now loads in 0.8 s. What do you do before publishing?

choices.label: Compare the old and new results on a few customers and months
choices.feedback: Right: a faster measure must still return the same numbers.

choices.label: Nothing, faster means correct
choices.feedback: A rewrite can change results, for example with duplicate rows.

exercises.answer: Measure first (Performance Analyzer, DAX Studio with a cold cache and Server Timings), fix the cause (context transition over the fact table), then check the results did not change.

exercises.q: On DAX.do (▶ button): add a Rank column to the products by revenue, with ties sharing a rank and no gap after them (expected: Laptop 1, Screen 2, Mouse 3, Desk 3). Start from this table (copy it after EVALUATE): VAR Products = DATATABLE ( "Product", STRING, "Revenue", DOUBLE, { { "Laptop", 2700 }, { "Screen", 900 }, { "Mouse", 600 }, { "Desk", 600 } } ) RETURN …
exercises.hint: RANKX ( table, expression, , DESC, DENSE ) inside ADDCOLUMNS. Then change DENSE to SKIP: what changes, and when would it show?
exercises.answer:
EVALUATE
VAR Products =
    DATATABLE (
        "Product", STRING, "Revenue", DOUBLE,
        {
            { "Laptop", 2700 },
            { "Screen", 900 },
            { "Mouse", 600 },
            { "Desk", 600 }
        }
    )
RETURN
    ADDCOLUMNS (
        Products,
        "Rank", RANKX ( Products, [Revenue], , DESC, DENSE )
    )
ORDER BY [Rank], [Product]

exercises.q: On DAX.do: add a Share column with each product's share of the total revenue of the table (expected: Laptop 0.5625, i.e. 56.25%). Start from this table (copy it after EVALUATE): VAR Products = DATATABLE ( "Product", STRING, "Revenue", DOUBLE, { { "Laptop", 2700 }, { "Screen", 900 }, { "Mouse", 600 }, { "Desk", 600 } } ) RETURN …
exercises.hint: In ADDCOLUMNS, [Revenue] is the current row; SUMX ( Products, [Revenue] ) walks the whole table again, whatever the current row. DIVIDE avoids a division by zero.
exercises.answer:
EVALUATE
VAR Products =
    DATATABLE (
        "Product", STRING, "Revenue", DOUBLE,
        {
            { "Laptop", 2700 },
            { "Screen", 900 },
            { "Mouse", 600 },
            { "Desk", 600 }
        }
    )
RETURN
    ADDCOLUMNS (
        Products,
        "Share", DIVIDE ( [Revenue], SUMX ( Products, [Revenue] ) )
    )
ORDER BY [Share] DESC

exercises.q: On DAX.do: return only the 2 products with the highest revenue. Start from this table (copy it after EVALUATE): VAR Products = DATATABLE ( "Product", STRING, "Revenue", DOUBLE, { { "Laptop", 2700 }, { "Screen", 900 }, { "Mouse", 600 }, { "Desk", 600 } } ) RETURN …
exercises.hint: TOPN ( n, table, order by, DESC ) returns a table. Try n = 3: Mouse and Desk tie at 600, so TOPN returns 4 rows. That is the tie behaviour to remember for Top N visuals.

exercises.q: On the practice model: Sales has one row per order line with Quantity and Net Price (the price of one unit after discount). Write [Total Sales], the amount sold, shown by year.
exercises.hint: There is no amount column: an iterator computes Quantity × Net Price on each line, then adds the results.
exercises.answer:
Total Sales =
SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Net Price] )
exercises.explain: SUMX evaluates the expression once per row of Sales (row context), then sums. In Power BI you could also add a calculated column and SUM it, but the measure keeps the model smaller. Every later exercise builds on this measure.

mistakes.says: This adds up the prices and ignores the quantity: a line of 3 units counts once. Compute Quantity × Net Price on each line with an iterator (SUMX).
Multiplying two totals is not the total of the products: multiply on each line first, then add up (SUMX).

exercises.q: The visual shows Product[Category] on rows. Write [Phones Sales]: the Phones row shows the sales of Phones, every other category row is blank, and the total shows the Phones sales.
exercises.hint: A plain boolean filter in CALCULATE overrides the row's category. Which modifier keeps it?
exercises.answer:
Phones Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], KEEPFILTERS ( Product[Category] = "Phones" ) )
exercises.explain: Product[Category] = "Phones" is short for FILTER ( ALL ( Product[Category] ), … ): on the Audio row it would replace Audio with Phones. KEEPFILTERS intersects instead: Audio ∩ Phones is empty, so the cell is blank. FILTER ( VALUES ( Product[Category] ), Product[Category] = "Phones" ) gives the same result.

mistakes.says: A filter argument replaces the row's filter on the same column: every category row shows the Phones total. KEEPFILTERS keeps the row's filter and intersects it with yours.

exercises.q: Categories on rows, Store[Channel] (Online, Shop) on columns. Write [Channel Share]: each cell shows the channel's share of its category's sales, so each row adds up to 100 %.
exercises.hint: The denominator is the sales of the same category in every channel: keep the category filter, remove only the channel one.
exercises.answer:
Channel Share =
DIVIDE (
    [Total Sales],
    CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS ( Store[Channel] ) )
)
exercises.explain: REMOVEFILTERS ( Store[Channel] ) (or ALL ( Store[Channel] ), or ALL ( Store )) drops the column's filter and keeps the row's category, so the denominator is the category total. On the total row there is no category filter: the cells become each channel's share of all sales.

mistakes.dax: DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( Sales ) ) )
mistakes.says: ALL ( Sales ) removes every filter that reaches Sales, the category included: you get each cell's share of the grand total. Remove only the channel filter.

mistakes.dax: DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] ) ) )
mistakes.says: This removes the category filter, so each cell is the category's share of the channel. The question asks for the channel's share of the category: remove the channel filter.

exercises.q: Write [Avg Sales per Customer], the average amount bought per customer in the period, counting only customers who bought something. Shown by year.
exercises.hint: Iterate the customers of the period and average [Total Sales] for each one.
exercises.answer:
Avg Sales per Customer =
AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ), [Total Sales] )
exercises.explain: VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ) lists the customers who bought in the year. For each one, [Total Sales] runs with context transition: the current customer becomes a filter, added to the year. AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), [Total Sales] ) also works, because AVERAGEX ignores the blanks of customers without sales; DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], DISTINCTCOUNT ( Sales[CustomerKey] ) ) gives the same number without an iterator.

mistakes.dax: AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ), SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Net Price] ) )
mistakes.says: Inside AVERAGEX, SUMX is not filtered by the current customer: an iterator only creates a row context, and only CALCULATE turns it into a filter (context transition). Call the measure [Total Sales] (a measure has a hidden CALCULATE) or wrap the SUMX in CALCULATE.

COUNTROWS ( Customer ) counts all 60 customers every year, even those who bought nothing: the year doesn't filter Customer (filters flow from Customer to Sales, not back). Count the customers found in Sales.

exercises.q: Write [Strong Months], the number of months whose sales are above 30,000, shown by year.
exercises.hint: FILTER a table of months with a condition on [Total Sales], then count its rows.
exercises.answer:
Strong Months =
COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Date'[Year Month] ), [Total Sales] > 30000 ) )
exercises.explain: VALUES ( 'Date'[Year Month] ) gives the months of the year in the cell. FILTER evaluates [Total Sales] for each month (context transition), keeps those above 30,000, and COUNTROWS counts them. A measure can't be used in a CALCULATE boolean filter, which is why FILTER is needed here.

mistakes.says: FILTER ( 'Date', … ) tests each day, and no single day reaches 30,000. Iterate the months: VALUES ( 'Date'[Year Month] ).

mistakes.dax: COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Date'[Year Month] ), SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Net Price] ) > 30000 ) )
mistakes.says: Without context transition, SUMX sees the sales of the whole year for every month, so every month passes the test. Use the measure [Total Sales].

exercises.q: Quarters on rows, years on columns. Write [Sales YoY %], the growth of sales against the same period of the previous year (blank when there is no previous year).
exercises.hint: Store the current sales and last year's sales in two variables, then DIVIDE the difference by last year.
exercises.answer:
Sales YoY % =
VAR Current = [Total Sales]
VAR LastYear = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( Current - LastYear, LastYear )
exercises.explain: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR moves the dates of the cell back one year (Q2 2025 → Q2 2024) and, as a filter on the date column of the date table, replaces the year and quarter filters. 2023 has no previous year in the model: LastYear is blank and DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error.

mistakes.says: This is the ratio this year ÷ last year (129 % for +29 %), not the growth. Subtract last year first: DIVIDE ( Current - LastYear, LastYear ).

mistakes.dax:
VAR LastYear = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], PREVIOUSYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
RETURN DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - LastYear, LastYear )
mistakes.says: PREVIOUSYEAR returns the whole previous year, so each quarter is compared with a full year. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR moves exactly the dates of the cell back one year.

exercises.q: Months of 2025 on rows (a slicer keeps 2025). Write [Sales YTD], the sales from 1 January to the end of the month of the row.
exercises.hint: A time intelligence function returns the dates from the start of the year to the last visible date.
exercises.answer:
Sales YTD =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], DATESYTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
exercises.explain: DATESYTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) returns the dates from 1 January to the last date visible in the cell; as a filter on the date table's date column it replaces the month filter. TOTALYTD ( [Total Sales], 'Date'[Date] ) is the same measure in one function. The total equals December's value: the whole year.

mistakes.says: This is a running total since the first date of the model (2023): it never restarts in January. DATESYTD (or TOTALYTD) restarts each year.
DATESMTD runs from the first day of the month: you get the month's sales again. Year to date is DATESYTD.

exercises.q: The months of 2024 on rows. Write [Sales 3M], the sales of the last three months ending with the month of the row (January 2024 includes November and December 2023).
exercises.hint: Start from the last visible date and go back three months.
exercises.answer:
Sales 3M =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -3, MONTH )
)
exercises.explain: MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ) is evaluated before CALCULATE changes anything: it is the last day of the row's month. DATESINPERIOD goes back three months from that day (from 31 March: 1 January to 31 March), and the filter on the date column replaces the 2024 slicer, which is why January 2024 can reach 2023.

mistakes.says: MIN gives the first day of the month, so the period ends there and misses most of the current month. Use MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), the last visible date.
DATEADD moves the month back, it doesn't widen it: you get the month three months earlier, alone. DATESINPERIOD returns a period of several months.

exercises.q: Product names on rows. Write [Product Rank], the rank of each product by sales (1 = best seller), blank on the total row.
exercises.hint: RANKX over all the product names, and ISINSCOPE to leave the total blank.
exercises.answer:
Product Rank =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ),
    RANKX ( ALL ( Product[Product] ), [Total Sales] )
)
exercises.explain: RANKX evaluates [Total Sales] for every product of ALL ( Product[Product] ) (context transition), then places the current row's value among them. On the total row the value is the grand total, which would rank 1: ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ) is FALSE there, so IF returns blank.

mistakes.says: On a product row, VALUES ( Product[Product] ) holds only that product, so every product is number 1. Rank against ALL ( Product[Product] ).

mistakes.dax: IF ( ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ), RANKX ( ALL ( Product ), [Total Sales] ) )
mistakes.says: ALL ( Product ) ranks against every row of the Product table: 24 colour variants, not the 22 product names of the visual (Aria Earbuds and Phone S come in two colours). Rank against ALL ( Product[Product] ).

exercises.q: Sales has two dates. Sales[OrderDate] → 'Date'[Date] is active, Sales[DeliveryDate] → 'Date'[Date] is inactive (see the model). Write [Sales by Delivery Date], the sales of each month of 2025 by delivery date.
exercises.hint: A CALCULATE modifier activates an existing inactive relationship for one measure.
exercises.answer:
Sales by Delivery Date =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], USERELATIONSHIP ( Sales[DeliveryDate], 'Date'[Date] ) )
exercises.explain: USERELATIONSHIP ( Sales[DeliveryDate], 'Date'[Date] ) makes the delivery relationship the active one inside this CALCULATE; the order-date relationship stops filtering. Orders placed at the end of December 2024 and delivered in January 2025 now count in January 2025.

mistakes.says: This is by order date: Sales[OrderDate] → 'Date'[Date] is the active relationship. Activate the inactive one for this measure with USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.

TREATAS adds a filter on the delivery date, but the active relationship still filters the order date: you only keep orders ordered and delivered in the same month. USERELATIONSHIP switches the relationship instead.

exercises.q: Years on rows, channels on columns. Write [Top 5 Customers Sales], the sales made by the 5 best customers of each cell (the best 5 of 2024 online may differ from the best 5 of 2025 in shops).
exercises.hint: TOPN builds a table of 5 customers; used as a CALCULATE filter, it keeps only them.
exercises.answer:
Top 5 Customers Sales =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    TOPN ( 5, VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ), [Total Sales] )
)
exercises.explain: Filter arguments are evaluated in the cell's filter context, before CALCULATE applies them: TOPN ranks the customers of that year and channel by [Total Sales] and returns 5. As a filter, the table keeps their sales only. Because each total is computed again, the total row shows the best 5 of the year in all channels, not the sum of the cells.

mistakes.dax: CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], TOPN ( 5, VALUES ( Sales[CustomerKey] ), SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Net Price] ) ) )
mistakes.says: Without context transition every customer gets the same value (the total of the cell), so TOPN keeps them all (ties are kept). Rank them by the measure [Total Sales].

mistakes.dax: CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], TOPN ( 5, ALL ( Customer[CustomerKey] ), CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( 'Date' ), ALL ( Store ) ) ) )
mistakes.says: This picks the 5 best customers of all time and all channels, then shows their sales in the cell. The question asks for the best 5 of each cell: rank with [Total Sales] in the cell's own filters.

exercises.q: Fix this measure: it should give the margin rate of each category but returns an error. Run it first to read the error.
exercises.hint: A measure has no current row: Sales[Quantity] alone can't be read. The cost needs an iterator, like the sales.
exercises.answer:
Margin % =
DIVIDE (
    [Total Sales] - SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Cost] ),
    [Total Sales]
)
exercises.explain: In a measure, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Cost] has no row context, hence "A single value for column 'Quantity' in table 'Sales' cannot be determined". SUMX gives each line a row context, multiplies, then adds up the cost. Store the result in a variable or a [Total Cost] measure for readability.
exercises.start:
Margin % =
DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Cost], [Total Sales] )

mistakes.dax: DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - SUM ( Sales[Unit Cost] ), [Total Sales] )
mistakes.says: SUM ( Sales[Unit Cost] ) adds one unit cost per line, whatever the quantity. Multiply by Sales[Quantity] on each line with SUMX.

interview.q: What is the difference between row context and filter context?
interview.a: The filter context is the set of filters on model columns that decides which rows a measure sees; it comes from the visual, slicers and filters, and propagates through relationships. The row context is the current row while DAX iterates a table, in a calculated column or an iterator such as SUMX. A row context does not filter other tables by itself: a SUM in a calculated column returns the grand total. CALCULATE converts a row context into a filter context through context transition.

interview.q: What is context transition, and when can it cause problems?
interview.a: When CALCULATE runs inside a row context, it turns the values of the current row into filters, and every measure reference has an implicit CALCULATE. That is why MAXX over customers with a measure works per customer. It causes problems on large tables, because it runs once per row and pushes work to the formula engine, and on tables without a unique key, where identical rows are filtered together and the result is double counted. I iterate dimension keys rather than the fact table.

interview.q: Explain the difference between ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLSELECTED and KEEPFILTERS.
interview.a: ALL and REMOVEFILTERS clear filters on a table or columns; REMOVEFILTERS is only a CALCULATE modifier and states the intent clearly, while ALL can also return a table to iterate. ALLSELECTED removes the filters of the visual's rows and columns but keeps those from slicers and page filters, which is what you want for a percentage of the visible total. KEEPFILTERS does the opposite kind of job: it makes a filter argument intersect with the existing filter instead of replacing it.

interview.q: Why is the total of my measure not the sum of the rows?
interview.a: Because a total is not a sum: the measure is evaluated again in the total's filter context, without the row filter. For additive measures it matches, but distinct counts, averages, ratios and anything with MAX or a condition do not add up. If the business wants the sum of the rows, I write it explicitly by iterating the row grain, for example SUMX ( VALUES ( Store[StoreKey] ), [Measure] ), and I check with ISINSCOPE what each level should show.

interview.q: How do you compute a closing balance or a stock level?
interview.a: Stock is semi-additive: it adds up across stores and products but not over time. I take the value on the last date of the period that has data, with LASTNONBLANK on the date column and a CALCULATE of the sum, and use it as a filter. Because stores may report on different last days, I compute it per store with SUMX over the store keys. LASTDATE would return the period's last date even when no snapshot exists, giving blanks.

interview.q: A fact table has an order date and a delivery date. How do you analyse both?
interview.a: I relate both columns to the same date table, keep the order date relationship active and the delivery one inactive, and write the delivery-date measures with USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE. That keeps one date table and one set of slicers. If users need to filter by both dates at once, for example orders placed in January and delivered in February, I add a second date dimension instead.

interview.q: How do you approach a slow DAX measure?
interview.a: I find the slow visual with Performance Analyzer, copy its query into DAX Studio, clear the cache and look at Server Timings. A high formula engine share, many storage engine queries or CallbackDataID usually point to an iteration with context transition over a big table, FILTER on a whole table or complex IF logic inside an iterator. I fix one thing at a time, measure again and check that the results are unchanged. If the model itself is large, I look at column cardinality with VertiPaq Analyzer.

interview.q: What are calculation groups and when would you use them?
interview.a: A calculation group is a table whose items are DAX expressions applied to whatever measure is in the visual, through SELECTEDMEASURE. A Time Calc group with Current, YTD, PY and YoY % replaces dozens of near-identical measures, and format string expressions keep percentages formatted. They can now be created in Power BI Desktop's model view. I watch out for items that make no sense on some measures, such as YoY % on a ratio, and exclude those with ISSELECTEDMEASURE.

playground.name: DAX.do
playground.about: DAX.do is a free DAX query playground made by SQLBI. The exercises marked ▶ build their own small table with DATATABLE, so they run as they are, whatever sample model DAX.do shows on the left.
